newsitem.title: USA: Convicted killer pleads for life.
newsitem.headline: Convicted killer pleads for life.

text.p: Convicted murderer and child molester Jesse Timmendequas, whose crime inspired so-called Megan's Laws around the nation, pleaded with a jury Wednesday to spare his life.
Timmendequas, 36, faces the death penalty for the 1994 rape and murder of 7-year-old Megan Kanka. The sentencing phase of his trial follows his conviction last month.

Timmendequas looked down at the floor as he apologised in a short statement for what he had done. He asked the jury to let him live so "some day I can understand why something like this could happen."

The Kanka family did not know Timmendequas was a twice-convicted child molester when he moved into their suburban Hamilton Township, New Jersey, neighbourhood. The attack inspired Megan's Laws that require child molesters to register with police when they move into a town.
In 1996 President Clinton signed a federal law making it easier to get information about released sex offenders.

Timmendequas was preceded on the witness stand by Kanka's father, Richard, who described the impact of his daughter's death. Kanka rehearsed his statement before the jury entered the courtroom to make sure he could speak without crying.
While he kept his composure, several jurors wiped away tears as he spoke.
"It has been almost three years since Megan's death and time has stood still for our family," Kanka said. "It feels as raw as if it happened yesterday."
He recalled his daughter as "gentle enough to have tea parties with her dolls and rugged enough to play in the mud with her brother's Tonka trucks."

Before she died, Megan had been sharing a bedroom with her sister Jessica and brother Jeremy because their house was under construction, he said. For months afterward, neither child could bear to sleep in that bedroom because of all its reminders, he said.
Jeremy has nightmares and his parents have found him screaming in his closet in the middle of the night, he said.
Timmendequas' lawyers, hoping to keep him off death row, have portrayed his childhood as "hellish" and filled with sexual and physical abuse that left him mentally ill.
In a closing argument, defence lawyer Roy Greenman said his client felt terrible remorse. He said he confessed almost immediately to police and was suicidal when he was jailed.

After a closing argument by the prosecution, jury deliberations were expected to begin on Thursday in Mercer County, New Jersey, Superior Court. Timmendequas has agreed to waive any possibility of parole if the jury decides he should not be executed.
